messages:
Sam: Quick question — thinking about a refactor where we shard control-plane responsibilities by account boundaries instead of a single multitenant CP. primary goals: reduce blast radius, let infra teams own CP creds, and simplify customer VPC networking.
Elaine: Do you mean full cross-account peering per customer or a hybrid with a central relay? both have tradeoffs.
Sam: Right. Two concrete options: 1) Cross-account peering + per-customer CP role and private endpoint in their account. 2) Central controlplane with VPC endpoints (PrivateLink) but cross-account IAM roles for control operations.
Thomas: Peering = more routing complexity (propagated routes, potential scale issues). PrivateLink = cost per ENI/endpoint, but simpler from route tables.
Mike: Also consider egress IPs for customer traffic. If CP is in their account, their outbound IPs look like their VPC -> easier for allowlists. Central CP + NAT = shared egress and might break some customer expectations.
Elaine: Agree. Another ops angle: cert rotation and CA trust. If we own central CP, we rotate centrally. Cross-account CP means we need an automated cert distribution mechanism into customer accounts.
Sam: That's a key point. For cross-account CP we sketched this bootstrap flow: assume role in customer account -> create endpoint + attach subnet -> deploy small agent -> perform mTLS handshake.
Jess: How do you feel about agent footprint? customers will push back on long-lived agents in their account.
Sam: Keep it tiny — just TLS handoff + healthchecks. No data plane heavy lifting unless requested.
Thomas: One more: monitoring and logs. Central CP = single observability plane. Cross-account CP = either pull logs from each account or require cross-account CloudWatch destinations. Both doable but adds config.
Mike: Cost tradeoff: PrivateLink endpoints cost $ and scales linearly with customers. Peering is free but operationally heavier. Cross-account CP has infra duplication and slightly higher infra cost per account.
Elaine: Security review note: least-privilege role we assume in customer account must be auditable. We should avoid granting broad EC2 or IAM perms. Maybe an endpoint operator role with narrow actions.
Sam: Rough pseudo for role policy we discussed:
```
Action: ["ec2:CreateNetworkInterface","ec2:ModifyNetworkInterfaceAttribute","ec2:DescribeVpcs","iam:PassRole"]
Resource: ["arn:aws:ec2:...","arn:aws:iam::...:role/endpoint-agent"]
```
Thomas: That looks reasonable. Also include a revoke/ttl flow so we can rotate the role.
infra-bot: Deploy job queued: cp-account-provisioner-spike -> build 0.3.2; ETA 2h :gear:
Jess: From a rollout perspective, I like starting with PrivateLink for enterprise customers (explicit accept, lower networking ops for us) and piloting cross-account peering for a handful of customers that need egress IP preservation.
Sam: Agreed. Pilot matrix: 3 customers on PrivateLink, 2 on cross-account CP, monitor latency, ops burden, and onboarding time.
Mike: Also log the number of route table entries and any route flaps during pilot. set a hard cap on peering count per region for automation.
Elaine: Follow-ups: I can draft a minimal IAM role + CA bootstrap doc. Sam — can you define the exact metrics for the pilot (onboard hours, incidents, cert rotations, cost delta)?
Sam: Yep, I'll post a short doc later today with the pilot metrics and an example onboarding checklist.
Jess: :thumbsup: thanks — this felt actionable.
Sam: Thanks everyone. tagging @Thomas and @Elaine for the role+security writeups.
